text:
The Setup
A university has 10 instructors who are cross-listed — they each teach one course in the Psychology department and one in Computer Science. At the end of the semester, students in both departments rate these instructors on a 4-point scale: Poor / Fair / Good / Excellent.
Each instructor has a latent (hidden) “teaching effectiveness” score that we never observe. We only see the ordinal rating. Now, both departments evaluate the same instructors, but their evaluation forms use different descriptions for the rating categories.
Psychology’s form:

Poor = “Did not meet basic expectations”
Fair = “Meets minimum expectations”
Good = “Consistently above average”
Excellent = “Outstanding in all respects”

Computer Science’s form:

Poor = “Did not meet basic expectations”
Fair = “Meets minimum expectations”
Good = “Solid and competent”
Excellent = “Solid and competent, with minor distinction”

Notice that in CS, students have to split hairs between “Good” and “Excellent” as the descriptions barely differ. This compresses the top two categories together. Consequently almost everyone who would be “Good” in Psychology ends up rated “Excellent” in CS, not because the teaching improved, but because the scale changed.
Here’s the simulation code. Read it carefully before running it.

set.seed(504)

# 10 cross-listed instructors with latent teaching effectiveness
instructors <- tibble(
  id = 1:10,
  effectiveness = rnorm(10, mean = 0, sd = 1.2)
)

# Each instructor rated by 20 students per department
ratings_latent <- instructors %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(latent = list(rnorm(20, mean = effectiveness, sd = 1))) %>%
  unnest(latent) %>%
  ungroup()

# --- THREE THRESHOLDS PRODUCE FOUR CATEGORIES ---

# Psychology: balanced scale
tau_psych <- c(-1.0, 0.0, 1.0)

# Computer Science: compressed top end
tau_cs <- c(-1.0, 0.0, 0.3)

ratings <- ratings_latent %>%
  mutate(
    eval_psych = case_when(
      latent <= tau_psych[1] ~ "Poor",
      latent <= tau_psych[2] ~ "Fair",
      latent <= tau_psych[3] ~ "Good",
      TRUE                   ~ "Excellent"
    ),
    eval_psych = ordered(eval_psych, levels = c("Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent")),
    
    eval_cs = case_when(
      latent <= tau_cs[1] ~ "Poor",
      latent <= tau_cs[2] ~ "Fair",
      latent <= tau_cs[3] ~ "Good",
      TRUE                ~ "Excellent"
    ),
    eval_cs = ordered(eval_cs, levels = c("Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent"))
  )

The thresholds \(\tau_1 = -1\), \(\tau_2 = 0\), \(\tau_3 = 1\) are on the latent “teaching effectiveness” scale — the continuous axis you generated but would never observe in real data. TipHint: What does plogis() do?





plogis() is the inverse logit. It converts log-cumulative-odds back to a probability: \(\text{plogis}(\tau) = \frac{e^\tau}{1 + e^\tau} = P(Y \leq k)\)




Suppose you want a rating distribution where 10% are Poor, 30% Fair, 40% Good, and 20% Excellent. What thresholds would produce this? text:
Mini-tutorial: avg_comparisons()
Marginal effects answer the question: “How much does the predicted probability of each category change when I shift one predictor, holding everything else constant?”
In OLS, the slope is the marginal effect, because one unit of X always produces β units of change in Y. That’s because the model predicts Y directly, with no transformation.
In any GLM with a nonlinear link (logistic regression, Poisson, ordinal, …), the slope and the marginal effect come apart. The model estimates β on a transformed scale (log-odds, log-counts), but the relationship between that scale and probability is a curve, not a line. The same β of 0.5 might shift a probability from 0.10 to 0.15 (a 5-point change) near the tails, but from 0.45 to 0.57 (a 12-point change) near the middle. The coefficient is identical in both cases, but its impact differs because the curve is steepest in the center and flat at the extremes.
For ordinal regression specifically, there’s an added wrinkle: the marginal effect is different for each category. Age might increase P(Rank 1) while simultaneously decreasing P(Rank 3), because probability must redistribute.
avg_comparisons() handles all of this. It computes the probability-scale effect at every observation, then averages — giving you one summary per category in percentage points.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Today

From logistic to ordinal
Motivating simulation: Loaded dice
Why not just use OLS?
The latent variable idea
Cumulative logit link
Thresholds and slopes
Application: Graduate school
Model fitting
Parameter interpretation
Proportional odds assumption
Model comparisons
Visualizing
Reporting

Here’s the roadmap. The first half is a simulation — just like the weighted coins we used for logistic regression, we’re going to build an ordinal outcome from scratch so you can see every piece of the model before we ever write a formula. The second half is a real dataset — graduate school applications — where we’ll fit actual models, compare them, and practice reporting.
Let’s start by connecting to what you already know.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Last time: Logistic regression
Binary outcomes: 0 or 1
. . .
We modeled P(Y = 1) using the logit link
\[\text{logit}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]
. . .
The logit mapped probabilities \((0, 1)\) → log-odds \((-\infty, +\infty)\), allowing a linear model
. . .
Today we extend this idea. What happens when your outcome has more than two ordered categories?
Quick recap.1) Last time we had binary outcomes — heads or tails, pass or fail, yes or no.2) We used the logit link to map probabilities, which live between 0 and 1, onto the full real line so that a linear model could work. THIS trick that made binary outcomes compatible with linear regression.
But what if your outcome isn’t just two categories?What if it’s ordered — like Strongly Disagree through Strongly Agree?That’s what we’ll be covering today.INTERACT: HAVE YOU USED ORDINAL DATA? DID YOU DO STATS WITH IT? ORDINAL OR VANILLA?

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Ordinal Response Variables
In psychology many variables have a natural ordering

Grades (e.g., A, B, C)
Education level (e.g., BA, MS, PhD)
Competitions (e.g., 1st, 2nd, 3rd)
Economic status (e.g., wealthy, middle class, poor)

Most common are Likert scale (“Lick-ert”) items
Ordinal data is everywhere in psychology. These are variables where the categories have a meaningful order, but the distances between them are unknown. Is the gap between an A and a B the same as between a B and a C? We don’t know — and that’s the whole problem.
The single most common source of ordinal data in psychology is the Likert scale — and yes, it’s pronounced “Lick-ert,” not “Lie-kert.”
Let me show you a fun example of how ordinal responses arise naturally.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: This is a cat, not a dog?
text:
This is a cat, not a dog?










Very likely to be a cat
Somewhat likely to be a cat
As likely to be cat or dog
Somewhat likely to be a dog
Very likely to be a dog

This is Button Idli. If I asked you to rate how likely this is to be a cat, you’d pick one of these five options. Notice that the responses have a clear order — 1 is “definitely cat” and 5 is “definitely dog” — but the spacing between them is subjective. Is the psychological distance between “very likely” and “somewhat likely” the same as between “somewhat likely” and “as likely”? Probably not.
J: As you progress from one to two to three to four to five, there’s an underlying latent variable — call it “catness” — that increases as you move up the scale. That latent variable is the hidden continuous thing the model is going to try to recover. Keep that idea in mind.
This is what makes ordinal data fundamentally different from continuous data, and it’s why we need a dedicated modeling approach.
So what do people actually do with data like this? Let’s look at the options.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Methods for analysis

Metric models (e.g., t-test, OLS)

Overestimate information in data; common & “simple”

Nonparametric (e.g., signed ranks)

Underestimate information; don’t scale well

Ordinal models ← today

Treat outcomes appropriately as ordered categories


There are basically three camps.
First, metric models — this is what almost everyone does. You treat your 1-through-5 scale as if it were a continuous number and run an ANOVA or a t-test. J: Nobody wants to give up their t-tests, ANOVAs, and regular regressions. There’s been a longstanding argument that if you have more than four categories, the variable is “close enough” to continuous and you can run models as you normally would. It’s common because it’s easy, but it makes assumptions we know are wrong.
Second, nonparametric tests — like the Wilcoxon — these make fewer assumptions, but they throw away information and don’t scale to complex designs.
Third, ordinal models — these are the Goldilocks option. They respect the ordering without pretending the distances are equal.
How bad can metric models really be? Let’s look at what the literature says.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
“What could possibly go wrong?”
Liddell and Kruschke (2018) surveyed 68 Psychology articles and found that every article used metric models on ordinal data.
. . .
Three main problems:

Response categories may not be (psychologically) equidistant
Responses can be non-normally distributed
Differences in variances of the underlying variable are treated inappropriately

. . .
Using metric models on ordinal data can lead to false alarms, failures to detect true effects, distorted effect sizes, and even inversions of effects.
This highlighted several issues which made the field start taking things more seriously
L&K surveyed 68 articles and every single one used metric models on ordinal outcomes. Every one!
hey searched for the word “Likert” across three top journals’ 2016 volumes:
JEP, Psych Science, PJSP
not used as often
L&K showed more. Consequences aren’t just theoretical.
They showed three specific problems.
First, the categories may not be equidistant
the psychological gap between “disagree” and “neutral” might be much larger than between “neutral” and “agree.”
Second, ordinal responses are often skewed
a lot of people pick the extreme ends, which violates normality.
Third, group differences in variance get confused with differences in means, which can flip the direction of your effect entirely.
So let’s actually see what happens when we use the wrong model. We’re going to simulate some ordinal data from scratch.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: Under the Hood: The Loaded Dice
text:
Under the Hood: The Loaded Dice
Just like we used weighted coins to understand logistic regression, we’re going to use loaded dice to understand ordinal regression. Same philosophy — build it, see it, then model it.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
The Loaded Dice
Easier to understand ordinal regression if we simulate it from scratch and watch the steps unfold.
Just like our weighted coins helped us understand logistic regression.
Remember the coin toss simulation?
We had 8 coins, each with a different amount of lead, and more lead meant a higher probability of heads.
We’re going to do the exact same thing, but now instead of two outcomes — heads or tails — we’ll have three ordered categories: Low, Medium, and High.
The big conceptual addition is the idea of thresholds
— invisible boundaries that chop a continuous latent variable into ordered categories.
That’s the core insight of ordinal regression, and the simulation will make it concrete.
Here’s the setup.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: Simulation with a Data Generating Process
text:
Simulation with a Data Generating Process
6 dice. 30 rolls each.
Each die has a lead weight. More lead → the die tends to produce higher scores on a continuous latent “quality” scale.
We then bin these latent scores into three ordered categories: Low, Medium, High.

set.seed(504)

# --- DATA GENERATING PROCESS ---
# Lead weight determines each die's latent mean
dice <- tibble(
  die         = 1:6,
  lead_weight = 1:6,
  latent_mean = c(-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0)
)

# TRUE thresholds (students will try to recover these)
tau1 <- -0.5   # boundary between Low and Medium
tau2 <-  1.0   # boundary between Medium and High

# Roll each die 30 times → continuous latent score → categorize
rolls <- dice %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(latent = list(rnorm(30, mean = latent_mean, sd = 1))) %>%
  unnest(latent) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(die) %>%
  mutate(roll = row_number()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    category = case_when(
      latent <= tau1 ~ "Low",
      latent <= tau2 ~ "Medium",
      TRUE           ~ "High"
    ),
    category = ordered(category, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
  )

Let me walk you through this.
We have 6 dice, each rolled 30 times.
Each die has a different amount of lead, from 1 gram to 6 grams.
More lead means the die’s latent “quality” score tends to be higher — just like more lead on the coin meant a higher probability of heads.
But here’s the key difference.
Each roll produces a continuous latent score [nobody sees]
— drawn from a normal distribution centered on that die’s latent mean.
Then we chop that continuous score into categories using two thresholds. If the latent score is below −0.5, we call it “Low.” Between −0.5 and 1.0, it’s “Medium.” Above 1.0, it’s “High.”
This is the data-generating process that ordinal regression assumes is happening in the real world. There’s a hidden continuous variable, and our categories are just a coarse binning of it.
J: This assumption — that we can map observed responses onto a continuous latent variable and divide it into bins using thresholds — is what’s called the latent variable interpretation of the model. I think it’s a very reasonable assumption for the kinds of variables we work with in psychology.
Write these numbers down!
tau 1 equals negative 0.5,
tau 2 equals 1.0. We’re going to see if our model can recover them.
Let me show you what this looks like.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: The truth you normally never see
text:
The truth you normally never see
Each point is a roll. The dashed lines are the true thresholds. Color = the category it falls into.









. . .
In real life, you never see this plot. You only see the colors — the categories. The y-axis is hidden from you. Ordinal regression’s job is to recover the thresholds and the effect of lead weight using only the categories.
This is the God’s-eye view —
the plot you’d never see in practice.
The y-axis is the latent continuous variable, the hidden quality score. Each dot is a single roll.

In real life, you never see the y-axis. You only see the colors. A survey participant picks “Agree” or “Strongly Agree” — you don’t see their underlying feeling on a continuous scale. Ordinal regression’s entire job is to recover this hidden structure from just the category labels.
So what does the data actually look like to us, the researchers?

What you actually observe

More weight → more “High” and fewer “Low.” The pattern is clear. How do we model it?
This is what your data actually looks like. No latent variable, no thresholds — just how many rolls fell into each category for each die. It’s a stacked bar chart.

You have groups, you have ordered categories, and you can see proportions shifting. The question is: what’s the best way to model this?

Anything new? Which probability?

This is the thing binary data didn’t have.

OLS can only handle one at a time — you’re forced to collapse an ordered outcome into a single binary split. That’s information loss. You had three categories and you threw two of them into a bucket. And you don’t really get predictions that make sense — so people don’t use it.

The “just code it 1-2-3” escape route makes things worse.

Students will think: “OK, so don’t model a probability — just predict the category number.”
That dodges the boundary issue but walks into a bigger one.
Now you’re assuming the gap between 1 and 2 equals the gap between 2 and 3. The numbers are labels you chose, not distances you measured.
Then the cumulative logit model is the answer to all three:
Logit link → probabilities stay in [0, 1] ✓
Models all cumulative splits simultaneously → no information loss ✓
Thresholds are estimated, not assumed equal → no equal-spacing assumption ✓
The punchline: Binary data had one problem with OLS. Ordinal data has three. The cumulative logit solves all of them.

Let me summarize the problems with OLS before we move on to the right model.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: Problems with the “treat it as numeric” approach
text:
Problems with the “treat it as numeric” approach
Three things went wrong

Assumes equal spacing — is the jump from Low → Medium the same as Medium → High? We don’t know, but OLS assumes it is.
Predicts impossible values — the line escapes the range of the data.
Wrong distributional assumptions — residuals are not normal, variance is not constant.

. . .
We need a model that respects the ordered nature of the outcome without assuming it’s metric.
Let me hammer these three points. First: equal spacing. When you code Low as 1, Medium as 2, High as 3, you’re asserting that the categories are evenly spaced. But think about a pain scale — the difference between “no pain” and “mild pain” is not the same as between “severe pain” and “worst pain imaginable.”
Second: impossible predictions. Just like logistic regression fixed the impossible-probability problem by using the logit link, ordinal regression will fix this by working with cumulative probabilities.
Third: distributional assumptions. The residuals from OLS on ordinal data violate normality and homoscedasticity. These aren’t minor technicalities — they affect your p-values and confidence intervals — your hypothesis tests and effect estimates.
So we need a new model. And the good news is, if you understood logistic regression, you already understand 80% of it. We just need one new idea: cumulative splits.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Cumulative Logit Model
Now we move from “what’s wrong with OLS” to “what’s the right model.” The key concept is cumulative splits — and they’re a natural extension of what you already know.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
The key idea: Cumulative splits
With binary logistic regression, we modeled one split:
\[\text{logit}(P(Y = 1)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]
. . .
With ordinal regression, we model multiple cumulative splits:

Split 1: P(Low) vs. P(Medium or High)
Split 2: P(Low or Medium) vs. P(High)

. . .
Each split is its own logistic regression — but they all share the same slope.
🔗 The connection
With 2 categories, ordinal regression is logistic regression. There’s 1 threshold, 1 slope.
With K categories, you get K − 1 thresholds but still just 1 slope per predictor. Think of it as running K − 1 logistic regressions simultaneously, forced to have the same slope.
Here’s the core idea, and it’s simpler than it looks. In logistic regression, we had one split — Y = 0 vs. Y = 1 — and we modeled it with one logit equation. In ordinal regression, we have multiple cumulative splits. With three categories, we get two splits: everything up to and including Low versus everything above it, and everything up to and including Medium versus everything above it.
Each split is literally a logistic regression. We take the cumulative probability — P of Y less than or equal to k — and apply the logit link. The trick is that all these logistic regressions share the same slope. They differ only in their intercepts — which we call thresholds.
Read the callout box with me. If you only have two categories, this reduces to exactly the logistic regression you already know. One threshold, one slope. So ordinal regression isn’t something new — it’s a generalization.
Let’s connect this back to the latent variable we saw in our dice simulation.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
The latent variable interpretation
There is a continuous latent variable \(\tilde{Y}\) (the “true score”) that gets categorized into bins by thresholds: \(\tau_1, \tau_2, \dots, \tau_{K-1}\)
In our dice simulation:

\(\tilde{Y}\) = the latent score
\(\tau_1 = -0.5\), \(\tau_2 = 1.0\)
Categories = Low, Medium, High

Remember the hidden y-axis from the dice simulation? The continuous score underneath the categories? The model assumes that’s real. Every ordinal response has a latent variable behind it — you just can’t see it. In our dice simulation, we actually got to see it — the latent score on the y-axis. In real life, you never see it, but the model assumes it’s there.
The thresholds are the cut points that divide this continuous variable into your observed categories. In our simulation, tau 1 was −0.5 and tau 2 was 1.0. With K categories, you need K − 1 thresholds. We always estimate J minus 1 thresholds, because once we know all but the last cut point, the final one is determined automatically.
Imagine a Gaussian getting sliced by vertical lines into bins. Each bin is an observed category. The model’s job is to estimate where those slices are and how the predictor shifts the curve.
Now let’s formalize what “cumulative” means here.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Ordered = Cumulative
We use the cumulative distribution to model ordered categories

Cumulative probability: \(P(Y \leq k)\)
Preserves the natural ordering
Always increasing: \(P(Y \leq 1) \leq P(Y \leq 2) \leq \dots\)


Richard McElreath
Why cumulative? Because cumulative probabilities naturally respect the ordering. The probability of being at or below category 2 is always at least as big as the probability of being at or below category 1. That monotonic structure is baked in, which is exactly what we want for ordered data.
The figure from McElreath illustrates this nicely. The bars on the left show the probability of each category. The bars on the right show the cumulative probabilities — each one stacks on top of the last, always growing, always reaching 1 at the top.
Let’s see where this sits in the GLM framework.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Generalized linear model
You saw this in the logistic regression lecture. Same skeleton — three components:
\[\begin{align*}
  Y_i & \sim \mathrm{Dist}(\mu_i, \tau) & \quad & \text{← Random component} \\
  g(\mu_i) & = \eta_i & \quad & \text{← Link function} \\
  \eta_i & = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \ldots & \quad & \text{← Linear predictor}
\end{align*}\]
. . .
Last time we filled in: Bernoulli distribution, logit link, linear predictor with one intercept and slopes.
. . .
What changes for ordinal data?
This is the same equation you saw two weeks ago. Nothing new yet — just the GLM skeleton. Three components: a distribution, a link function, and a linear predictor. Last time we plugged in Bernoulli for the distribution, logit for the link, and got logistic regression.
The question is: what do we plug in this time?
Let me show you.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: Ordinal regression: Filling in the GLM
text:
Ordinal regression: Filling in the GLM
\[\begin{align*}
  Y_i & \sim \color{#d63031}{\mathrm{Cumulative}}(\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_K) & \quad & \color{#d63031}{\text{← Ordinal outcome (K ordered categories)}} \\[8pt]
  \color{#2d3436}{g(\mu_i)} & = \color{#0984e3}{\mathrm{logit}} & \quad & \color{#0984e3}{\text{← Same link as logistic regression}} \\[8pt]
  \eta_i & = \color{#00b894}{\alpha_k - (\beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \ldots)} & \quad & \color{#00b894}{\text{← Thresholds + slopes}}
\end{align*}\]
. . .

Distribution — Models cumulative probability \(P(Y \leq k)\) — preserves the ordering
Link — Logit — identical to logistic regression. Nothing new here.
Linear predictor — \(K-1\) thresholds \(\alpha_k\) (one per split) + shared slopes \(\beta\) (proportional odds)

Now we fill in the blanks. Three changes from logistic regression — and only one of them is actually new.
Cumulative logit model (notation) {.smaller}.
The distribution — in red. Instead of Bernoulli (binary), we have a cumulative distribution over K ordered categories. The model works with cumulative probabilities — P of Y less than or equal to k — which naturally preserves the ordering. This is the new part.
The link function — in blue. It’s the logit. Exactly the same logit as logistic regression. Nothing new to learn here. You already know this.
The linear predictor — in green. This is where the thresholds live. Instead of one intercept, you have K minus 1 thresholds — one for each cumulative split. And the slopes are shared across all splits. That shared slope is the proportional odds assumption. Two things that are new: multiple intercepts, and the subtraction sign.
So of the three GLM components, one is new, one is identical, and one is a natural extension. That’s why ordinal regression is easier than it looks.
Now let’s define the cumulative odds and the cumulative logit formally.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Cumulative log-odds







Symbol
Meaning




\(P_k\)
Probability of being in category k


\(C_{pk}\)
Cumulative probability of being in category k or lower


1 − \(C_{pk}\)
Probability of being above category k



\[\textrm{Cumulative Odds} = \frac{P(Y \leq k)}{P(Y > k)} = \frac{C_{pk}}{1-C_{pk}}\]
. . .
Take the log to get the cumulative logit:
\[\log\left(\frac{C_{pk}}{1-C_{pk}}\right)\]
. . .
🏷️ Jargon Alert
Cumulative logit = cumulative log-odds = the same logit link you already know, just applied to cumulative probabilities.
Let’s build this up step by step, just like we did for logistic regression. The cumulative probability is P of Y less than or equal to k — the probability of being in category k or any lower category. The cumulative odds are the ratio of that probability to its complement — the probability of being above category k. And the cumulative logit is just the log of those odds.
This is exactly the same logit you already know. The only difference is that instead of modeling P(Y = 1), we’re modeling P(Y ≤ k). Same link function, same transformation, same interpretation of log-odds. Just applied cumulatively.
Let’s look at McElreath’s visualization of how this works.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Cumulative logit model
Richard McElreath
This figure from McElreath shows the cumulative probabilities being mapped to the log-odds scale. On the left, you have the cumulative probabilities — they go from 0 to 1, always increasing. On the right, those get transformed to log-odds, which live on the full real line.
Each cumulative split gets its own log-odds value — and those are the thresholds in our model. The threshold between category 1 and everything above it, the threshold between categories 1-and-2 and everything above, and so on. Here the outcomes 1 through 7 are labeled on the right — each one maps to a point on the log-odds axis.
The next figure adds the visual connection between the two panels.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Cumulative logit model
Richard McElreath
Same figure, but now with dashed horizontal lines connecting the cumulative proportions on the left to their corresponding points on the log-odds scale on the right. This makes the mapping visible — you can trace each cumulative bar across to its log-odds value.
The next figure labels these points as the model’s cutpoints.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Cumulative logit model
Richard McElreath
Now the payoff. The points on the log-odds axis are labeled as cutpoints — α₁ through α₆. These are exactly the threshold parameters that the model estimates. With 7 categories, you get 6 cutpoints. The last category always goes to positive infinity.
This is what the model estimates. Each cutpoint is a log-cumulative-odds value — the same thing you computed by hand for the 3-gram die. A predictor shifts all these cutpoints simultaneously — that’s the proportional odds assumption.
Now let’s write down the actual equation.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
The model equation
\[\log \left(\frac{P(Y \leq k)}{P(Y > k)}\right) = \alpha_k - \beta X\]
\[\begin{array}{rcl} L_1 &=& \alpha_1 - \beta_1 x_1 - \cdots - \beta_p X_p\\ L_2 &=& \alpha_2 - \beta_1 x_1 - \cdots - \beta_p X_p \\ L_{J-1} &=& \alpha_{J-1} - \beta_1 x_1 - \cdots - \beta_p X_p \end{array}\]

We estimate J − 1 equations simultaneously
Each equation has a different intercept \(\alpha_k\) (the thresholds/cut points)
But a common slope \(\beta\) ← this is the proportional odds assumption
Intercepts are always ordered: \(\alpha_1 < \alpha_2 < \dots\)

Here’s the full equation. On the left side: the cumulative logit — log-odds of being at or below category k. On the right side: a threshold alpha k, minus the linear predictor.
Three things to notice. First: we’re estimating J minus 1 equations simultaneously — one for each cumulative split. With 3 categories, that’s 2 equations. Second: each equation has its own intercept, the threshold alpha k, but they all share the same slope beta. That shared slope is the proportional odds assumption — the effect of the predictor is the same no matter which cumulative split you’re looking at. Third: the thresholds are always ordered — alpha 1 is always less than alpha 2.
For our dice: J = 3 categories, so we estimate 2 thresholds and 1 slope. That’s 3 parameters total to describe the entire ordinal relationship. Very parsimonious.
Let me break down what each piece means in plain language.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
What do the pieces mean?
\(\alpha_k\) (thresholds/intercepts/cut-offs):

Log-odds of falling at or below category \(k\) when all predictors = 0
These are the ordinal equivalent of \(\beta_0\) in logistic regression

\(\beta\) (slopes):

Effect of the predictor on the log-odds of being in a higher category
Shared across all cumulative splits

The \(-\) sign:

Convention so that a positive \(\beta\) means higher X → higher category

Let me translate each piece. The thresholds, alpha k, are like intercepts. They tell you the log-odds of being at or below category k when your predictor is zero. Think of them as the “baseline cut points” of your ordinal scale. In logistic regression, you had one intercept; here you have K minus 1 of them.
The slope, beta, is the effect of the predictor. Just like in logistic regression, a one-unit increase in X changes the log-odds by beta. The difference is that this change applies to every cumulative split equally. That’s the power and the constraint of the proportional odds model.
The subtraction sign is a convention — it’s there so that a positive beta means higher X leads to higher categories. Some software uses addition, which flips the sign. Always check your software’s convention.
J: If we used the standard additive parameterization, a more positive log odds would actually correspond to a higher probability of being in a lower category, which is counterintuitive. The subtraction is there to make interpretation go in the natural direction. The packages we’re using today — ordinal::clm() and MASS::polr() — both use subtraction, so positive means higher.
Now let me show you visually what the thresholds and slopes are doing.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: Thresholds are where the latent variable gets cut into categories.
text:
Thresholds are where the latent variable gets cut into categories.









. . .
Close thresholds → few people land in the middle category. Far-apart thresholds → the middle category captures a wide range.
These two panels show the same latent distribution, but with different thresholds. On the left, the thresholds are close together — the middle category, Medium, covers only a narrow band of the latent variable. Most people end up in either Low or High. Think of a scale where “neutral” almost never gets picked.
On the right, the thresholds are far apart — the middle category is wide and absorbs a lot of the distribution. Most people end up in Medium. Think of a scale where people cluster in the middle and extremes are rare.
The thresholds are properties of the measurement scale, not the predictor. They tell you about how your response categories carve up the latent continuum. The model estimates them — you don’t have to assume equal spacing.
Now what about the slope?

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
What the slope does
The slope \(\beta\) shifts the entire latent distribution along the x-axis — the thresholds stay put.









. . .
A positive \(\beta\) shifts the distribution right, increasing P(higher categories). The thresholds \(\alpha_k\) don’t move — they’re properties of the response scale, not the predictor.
This is the visual that ties it all together. The thresholds — the dashed vertical lines — stay fixed. They’re at −0.5 and 1.0 in both panels. What changes is the distribution’s position.
On the left: low lead weight. The distribution is shifted left, so most of the area falls below the first threshold — most rolls are “Low.” On the right: high lead weight. The distribution is shifted right, so most of the area is above the second threshold — most rolls are “High.”
The slope beta controls how much the distribution shifts per unit of the predictor. A large positive beta means a big rightward shift — a strong effect. A small beta means barely any shift.
This is conceptually identical to what the intercept and slope did in logistic regression — they shifted the S-curve. Here, they shift the latent distribution relative to fixed thresholds.
There’s a parametrization detail I need to mention briefly.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Parametrization note
With subtraction convention (\(\alpha_k - \beta X\)):

Positive \(\beta\) → higher probability of being in higher categories

With addition convention (\(\alpha_k + \beta X\)):

Positive \(\beta\) → higher probability of being in lower categories

. . .
ordinal::clm() uses subtraction by default (positive = higher). MASS::polr() also uses subtraction. Just check the documentation for whatever package you use.
Quick practical note. Different software uses different sign conventions. The clm function we’re using today and polr both use the subtraction convention — meaning a positive coefficient pushes observations toward higher categories, which is the intuitive direction. Some software uses addition, which flips the interpretation.
Whenever you use a new package for ordinal regression, check this. It’s the most common source of sign confusion. If your coefficient is positive but the predicted probabilities seem to go the wrong way, the sign convention is probably the issue.

These threshold estimates are the log-cumulative-odds pooled across all six dice — the same quantity you just computed by hand, but now averaged over the whole dataset. When we add lead_weight as a predictor next, watch how the thresholds and model fit change.

Look at the output. You get two numbers — one for Low|Medium and one for Medium|High. These are the log-cumulative-odds of being at or below each category, pooled across all dice. They’re the “baseline” cut points when we don’t know anything about lead weight.

The thresholds in the predictor model will be the log-cumulative-odds when lead_weight = 0, and the slope will tell you how much the distribution shifts per gram of lead. The intercept-only model is your reference point for understanding what changed.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Proportional odds assumption
The key assumption: the slope is equal across all cumulative splits
In our dice model: the effect of lead weight on the log-odds of \(Y \leq\) Low vs. \(Y >\) Low is the same as the effect on \(Y \leq\) Medium vs. \(Y >\) Medium
. . .
If this assumption holds, you only need one slope per predictor — massive parsimony. If it doesn’t hold, consider partial proportional odds or multinomial models.
This is the single most important assumption of the model, and it’s the one that gives it its name. The proportional odds assumption says: the effect of a predictor is the same for every cumulative split. The slope doesn’t change depending on where you draw the line.
J: The constant slope across equations is what makes interpretation straightforward — a higher beta means a higher chance of being in a higher category, period. If the slopes are not constant — if the lines are not parallel — this interpretation breaks down, which complicates things considerably.
Think about what this means for our dice. The effect of lead weight on the odds of being in Low versus Medium-or-High is the same as the effect on Low-or-Medium versus High. One slope captures the whole story. That’s incredibly parsimonious — but it’s also a strong assumption.
If it’s violated — if, say, lead weight has a huge effect on moving from Low to Medium but almost no effect on moving from Medium to High — then you need a model that allows different slopes for different splits. We’ll talk about how to test this.
Let me mention briefly what happens when it breaks.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
FYI: Partial proportional odds model
Is it fair to say the effect of your predictor stays the same across all category transitions?
. . .
Examples of when this breaks down:

Test prep might help more for moving from F → D than from A− → A
Age might strongly affect moving from “poor” → “fair” health but less so from “good” → “excellent”
Ceiling effects

. . .
How to know?

Likelihood ratio test comparing the two types of models
Big difference ⇒ the proportional assumption is probably wrong

Here are some real examples where proportional odds breaks down. Test prep might help a failing student a lot but have almost no effect at the top of the scale — that’s a ceiling effect. Age might strongly predict moving from poor to fair health, but the jump from good to excellent might depend more on genetics than age. In both cases, the slope is different for different cumulative splits.
You test this with a likelihood ratio test — compare the proportional odds model (one slope) to a model that allows different slopes at each split. If the more flexible model fits significantly better, the proportional odds assumption is probably wrong.
When it is wrong, you have options: partial proportional odds, multinomial regression, or adjacent category models. We’ll see the Brant test for this in the applied example.

text:
Testing proportional odds assumption
brant test: compares the full proportional odds model to one that relaxes the assumption
You want a non-significant \(\chi^2\) test

library(gofcat)
brant.test(ols1)


Brant Test:
           chi-sq   df   pr(>chi)
Omnibus     0.017    1        0.9
pared1      0.017    1        0.9

H0: Proportional odds assumption holds


The Brant test is the standard frequentist test for the proportional odds assumption. It compares our model — which constrains the slope to be equal across all cumulative splits — to a model that allows different slopes. If the test is significant, the assumption is violated — the slopes are meaningfully different across splits.
J: Specifically, the Brant test performs a chi-square comparison between a model with one common slope and a model with separate slopes for each threshold. We want the chi-square to be non-significant — that’s evidence that the proportional odds assumption holds and our single-slope model is adequate.
You want a non-significant result here. That means the proportional odds model is adequate — the simplification of having one shared slope is defensible.
Look at the p-value. Is it significant?
If it were violated, here’s what you’d do.

title: Ordinal Regression
section: If the proportional odds test is violated
text:
If the proportional odds test is violated
Several options:

Multinomial regression — use lowest level as reference; no ordering assumed
Adjacent category model — model transitions between neighboring categories
Non-proportional odds (NPO) model — allow slopes to vary by split


# In VGAM: NPO model
library(VGAM)
ols_npo <- vglm(apply ~ pared, family = cumulative(parallel = FALSE, reverse = TRUE), data = dat)

If the Brant test is significant, you have three main options. Multinomial regression throws away the ordering information and treats the categories as unordered — it’s the most flexible but also the least efficient. Adjacent category models model each transition between neighboring categories separately. Non-proportional odds models keep the ordinal structure but allow different slopes at each split — this is often the best compromise.
The code here shows how to fit a non-proportional odds model in VGAM — you set parallel = FALSE to let the slopes vary.
J: The non-proportional odds model is fit using vgam() from the VGAM package with parallel = FALSE. The output will show J minus 1 slopes rather than one — one for each cumulative split — and you can interpret each coefficient the same way as in the standard ordinal model, just now they’re allowed to differ.
In practice, a mildly significant Brant test with similar-looking slopes across splits is often not worth abandoning proportional odds for. Use your judgment — the proportional odds model is more interpretable.

RM: Seeing the full redistribution
A predictor doesn’t push someone into a specific category — it shifts their latent score, which redistributes probability across all categories simultaneously.

predictions(ols2, 
            newdata = datagrid(gpa = c(2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0), 
                               pared = "0", public = "0")) %>%
  mutate(gpa_label = paste0("GPA = ", gpa)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = estimate, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~gpa_label, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("unlikely" = color_low, 
                                "somewhat likely" = color_med, 
                                "very likely" = color_high),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Response category", y = "Predicted probability",
       title = "How probability mass redistributes as GPA increases",
       subtitle = "Non-college-educated parent, private school") +
  theme_lucid(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))








. . .
This is what the model predicts, not the raw data. As GPA rises, probability drains from “unlikely” and flows into “somewhat likely” and “very likely.” All three categories change simultaneously — that’s the ordinal redistribution.
RM: This visualization comes from McElreath’s strongest pedagogical conviction: never just stare at coefficient tables — plot the predicted probabilities. The stacked area plot on the previous slide was useful, but this version is more direct. You can see the full probability distribution across all three response categories, side by side, for four representative GPA values.
Watch what happens as you move left to right. At GPA = 2.5, the “unlikely” bar dominates — most of the probability mass is there. At GPA = 3.0, it starts to shrink. By GPA = 4.0, “unlikely” has dropped substantially and “somewhat likely” and “very likely” have grown.
The key insight — and this is straight from McElreath — is that a predictor doesn’t push someone into a specific category. It shifts their underlying latent score, which probabilistically redistributes them across all categories simultaneously. The bars move as a system. Probability drains from one end and flows to the other. That’s what ordinal regression is capturing.
The error bars are 95% confidence intervals — notice they’re wider at the extremes of GPA where we have less data. This is the kind of figure that belongs in a paper or presentation, because it communicates the practical meaning of your model without requiring anyone to think about log-odds.

Model fit
Pseudo-\(R^2\)

r2_mcfadden(ols2)

# R2 for Generalized Linear Regression
       R2: 0.033
  adj. R2: 0.030


. . .
Not “explained variance” — but a ratio indicating how much better the model fits than an intercept-only model
McFadden’s pseudo-R-squared for ordinal regression. This is not explained variance — don’t interpret it the way you would an R-squared from OLS. It’s a ratio comparing the log-likelihood of your model to the log-likelihood of an intercept-only model. Values tend to be much lower than OLS R-squared — a McFadden’s R-squared of 0.2 to 0.4 is generally considered quite good.
Our value is quite small, which means these predictors explain only a modest amount of the variation in application intentions. That’s not unusual in social science — there are many unmeasured factors that influence a decision like this.

text:
Model diagnostics
No easystats functions for ordinal models :(
sure package: surrogate residuals — based on continuous residuals
Check normality, linearity, homoscedasticity

library(sure)
library(gridExtra)

set.seed(1225)

# Reduced nsim for faster rendering
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
  autoplot.clm(ols2, nsim = 50, what = "qq"),
  autoplot.clm(ols2, nsim = 50, what = "fitted", alpha = 0.5),
  ncol = 2
)








For multicollinearity, check correlations between predictor variables directly.
Unfortunately, the easystats diagnostic functions don’t work for ordinal models. The sure package fills the gap with surrogate residuals — these are simulated continuous residuals that let you do the familiar QQ plots and residual-vs-fitted plots.
J: What are surrogate residuals? They’re continuous residuals derived by mapping the ordinal outcome onto a continuous space — essentially reverse-engineering a continuous variable from your ordinal data so that standard diagnostic tools become applicable. For the Q-Q plot: all points falling on the line indicates normality is not violated. For the linearity plot: the smoothed line should be roughly flat at zero. For the box plots checking homoscedasticity: the boxes should be approximately overlapping.
The QQ plot on the left checks normality of the latent variable. If the points follow the diagonal, you’re fine. The residual-vs-fitted plot on the right checks for patterns — you want a random scatter, not a funnel or a curve.
J: For multicollinearity, you can’t use easystats directly with clm models. Instead, inspect correlations between predictors using Spearman rank correlations, which are more appropriate for ordinal and non-normal data than Pearson correlations. You can also compute VIFs from a regular linear model with the same predictors as a rough check.
Now let’s cover the formal assumptions.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Assumptions
Quick summary of what you need to check and what you don’t.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Ordinal regression assumptions

✅ Outcome is ordinal (ordered categories)
✅ Observations are independent
✅ Proportional odds (parallel slopes across cumulative splits)
✅ Linearity in the log-odds (for continuous predictors)
No normality assumptions for residuals
Homogeneity of variance

Four assumptions to check, two to celebrate. First, the outcome must be ordinal — obvious, but make sure your factor levels are correctly ordered. Second, independence — no repeated measures or clustering without accounting for it. Third, proportional odds — test with Brant or a likelihood ratio test. Fourth, linearity in the log-odds for continuous predictors — check with the surrogate residual plots.
The two crossed-out lines are things you don’t need to worry about. No normality assumption for observed residuals, and no homoscedasticity requirement. Those are OLS problems that the ordinal model avoids.
One more thing before we wrap up — what if your data has clustering?

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Multilevel ordinal regressions
For repeated measures or clustered/nested designs:

# Use clmm() from the ordinal package
ols_multilevel <- ordinal::clmm(
  apply ~ pared + gpa + (1 | school_id),
  data = dat
)

If you have repeated measures — say, the same person rates multiple items on a Likert scale — or nested data — students within schools — you need clmm instead of clm. The syntax is just like lmer — you add random effects in parentheses.
This is the same extension we made from glm to glmer for multilevel logistic regression. The ordinal package makes this seamless.
J: The ordinal package provides clmm(), which uses the same syntax as lme4. It is straightforward to scale up from clm to clmm for these more complex designs — you just add your random effects specification and everything else stays the same.
Now let’s close with reporting — how do you write this up?
Everything you’ve done is pointless if you can’t communicate it. Let’s talk about writing this up.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Sample write-up
A proportional odds model with a logit link (estimated using ML) was used to investigate factors influencing undergraduates’ likelihood of applying to graduate school (“unlikely,” “somewhat likely,” “very likely”). The overall model fit was modest, McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) = .03. Parent education significantly predicted application likelihood, b = 1.05, z = 3.94, p < .001, OR = 2.85, 95% CI [1.55, 5.28]. Students with college-educated parents had roughly 185% higher odds of applying. Whether students attended public or private school did not significantly predict application likelihood, b = −0.06, z = −0.20, p = .844, OR = 0.94. GPA was also a significant predictor, b = 0.62, z = 2.36, p = .018, OR = 1.85. Each one-point increase in GPA was associated with 85% higher odds of applying.
Here’s a sample write-up. Notice the structure: name the model, report fit, then go predictor by predictor with log-odds, z-values, p-values, odds ratios, and CIs. Each predictor gets a plain-language interpretation after the numbers.
A few things to note: We say “proportional odds model with a logit link” — that tells readers exactly what we did. We report both the log-odds coefficient and the odds ratio with CI — give readers both metrics. And we translate the odds ratio into a percentage — “185% higher odds” is more accessible than “OR = 2.85.”
What’s missing from this write-up that you should add? The proportional odds test results, the sample size, the distribution across categories, and ideally the marginal effects.
Here’s the full checklist.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Reporting checklist

Report the model type (proportional odds / cumulative logit) and estimation method
Report log-odds coefficients and odds ratios with 95% CIs
Report thresholds (or note they are available)
Report a measure of model fit (McFadden pseudo-\(R^2\))
Test and report the proportional odds assumption (Brant test or LRT)
Consider reporting marginal effects / predicted probabilities for each category
Include sample size and distribution across response categories
Mention diagnostics (surrogate residuals, multicollinearity)

Your reporting checklist — keep this handy for your assignments and papers. The items in bold are the ones that get most often forgotten. People report the coefficients but forget to test proportional odds. They report odds ratios but not marginal effects. They don’t mention the category distribution.
Compare this to the logistic regression checklist from last time — it’s very similar, with two additions: the proportional odds test and the category distribution. The model type and fit measures are analogous.
And finally, the mistakes to avoid.

title: Ordinal Regression
text:
Common Mistakes

Treating ordinal data as continuous — running OLS or t-tests on Likert scales
Forgetting that coefficients are in cumulative log-odds, not probabilities
Confusing thresholds with slopes — thresholds are intercepts for each cumulative split, not effects of predictors
Ignoring the proportional odds assumption — Always test it; if it fails, consider partial proportional odds or multinomial
Interpreting odds ratios as probability ratios — OR = 3 means 3× the odds, not 3× the probability
Not visualizing predicted probabilities per category — Log-odds and ORs are hard to interpret; always plot plot_predictions()

Let me go through these one at a time. Number one: treating ordinal data as continuous. This is the most common mistake in psychology. We spent the first part of today showing you exactly why it fails — don’t do it.
Number two: forgetting the metric. Your coefficients are cumulative log-odds, not probabilities. Always convert when communicating results.
Number three: confusing thresholds and slopes. Students often look at the threshold estimates and try to interpret them as effects. They’re not — they’re properties of the measurement scale. The slopes are the effects.
Number four: not testing proportional odds. Always run the Brant test. It takes one line of code.
Number five: odds ratios are not probability ratios. OR = 3 does not mean “three times more likely.” It means three times the odds. These are different, especially when probabilities are far from 0.5.
Number six: not plotting. Ordinal regression outputs are hard to interpret from numbers alone. Always make the predicted probability plots — they’re what your audience will actually understand.
J: If you are using ordinal variables in your research, you really should be using ordinal regression. Hopefully by the end of today you’ll shift your focus from metric models toward ordinal models when working with this type of data.
That’s everything. The core message: ordinal regression is logistic regression extended to more than two ordered categories, with thresholds slicing a latent continuum. The proportional odds assumption gives you one slope per predictor. Test it, visualize it, report it properly.
